A good structure solves both: you always know how to start, what comes next and how to finish. This guide gives you a TOEFL speaking template for each task in the current TOEFL iBT format (updated January 2026), with sample answers you can study and adapt.
The current TOEFL Speaking tasks at a glance
The Speaking section now takes about 8 minutes and has two task types:

Each item is scored out of 5, and the section is reported on the 1 to 6 band scale. The old independent and integrated speaking tasks, with reading passages and lectures to summarise, are no longer part of the test, so templates built for those tasks are out of date.
A template is only half the job. Your delivery (pace, pronunciation, fluency) matters just as much; we cover that in our TOEFL speaking tips for a clear and confident voice.
Listen and Repeat: a chunking structure
There is nothing to plan in this task, but there is still a method. Long sentences are impossible to remember word by word, so break them into units of meaning:

Who or what (the subject): “The students in the biology lab …”
Action (the verb group): “… have to submit their reports …”
Extra detail (time, place, reason): “… before the end of the week.”

While you listen, picture these three chunks. When you speak, keep the same rhythm and stress you heard. If you miss a word, keep going and complete the sentence naturally; stopping halfway costs more.
A TOEFL speaking template for Take an Interview
The interview questions move from simple to more demanding. According to ETS, prompts are designed to draw out descriptions, explanations, opinions, suggestions, predictions and narrations. One flexible core structure works for all of them:

Answer the question directly in the first sentence.
Reason: give one clear reason.
Example: support it with a short, specific example from your own life.
Wrap up: one sentence that links back to the question.

This is the PREP method (Point, Reason, Example, Point) adapted for interview questions. It keeps you focused and stops you from running out of ideas halfway through.

“Some students prefer to study alone, while others prefer study groups. Which do you prefer, and why?”

So for me, group study is more effective, as long as the group stays small and focused.

x:
Describe Image worries many PTE students because you get only a few seconds to make sense of a chart and then you have to talk about it without stopping. The good news is that it rewards a clear, repeatable approach. In this guide we share a flexible PTE describe image template for 2026, explain how Pearson scores the task, and walk through two sample answers: one for a bar chart and one for a process diagram.
How Describe Image works in PTE Academic
Describe Image sits in Part 1 (Speaking and Writing) of PTE Academic. An image appears on screen and you have 25 seconds to study it and prepare. After a short tone the microphone opens and you have 40 seconds to describe it. You can record your answer only once.
The image can be a bar chart, line graph, pie chart, table, map, process diagram or a photograph. Pearson advises aiming for 30 to 40 seconds of speech.
How your answer is scored
Pearson scores Describe Image on three traits:

Content: whether you accurately describe the main elements of the image, including relationships, trends and a sensible conclusion or implication.
Oral fluency: whether your rhythm and phrasing are smooth. Hesitations, repetitions and false starts lower this score.
Pronunciation: whether your speech is easily understood. Indian and other regional accents are fine as long as you are clear.

One rule matters more than any other. Pearson warns that memorised responses or templated sentences that are not about the image can earn zero for content, and if content scores zero, fluency and pronunciation are not scored either. So a “template” must be a structure you fill with real details from the image, never a paragraph you recite.
A flexible PTE describe image template for 2026
Think of the template as four slots. Each slot is a job to do, and the words you use change with every image.

Topic sentence (about 5 seconds): say what the image shows, using its own title and labels. “This bar chart compares the number of international students in four Australian cities in 2015 and 2025.”
Main feature (about 10 seconds): the single most important point. The highest value, the biggest change or the first stage of a process.
Two or three supporting details (about 15 to 20 seconds): a comparison, a lowest value, a trend or the next stages. Use real numbers from the image.
Conclusion or implication (about 5 seconds): a short, logical takeaway. “Overall, the figures suggest that demand grew fastest in Melbourne.”

You do not need to mention everything. Three or four key data points are enough. Pearson also advises against spending too long on labels or adding personal opinions.
Useful phrases you can adapt

Comparing: “is roughly twice as high as”, “is slightly lower than”, “the gap between X and Y is about 20 per cent”.
Trends: “rose steadily from … to …”, “fell sharply after …”, “remained stable at around …”.
Processes: “The process begins with …”, “Next …”, “Once this is done …”, “Finally …”.
Conclusions: “Overall, it is clear that …”, “This suggests that …”.

These phrases are building blocks for your PTE describe image template, not a script. Combine them with the actual figures and labels in front of you.
Sample answer 1: bar chart
Image: a bar chart titled “Daily screen time of students by age group”, showing hours per day for four groups: 10 to 12 years (3 hours), 13 to 15 years (5 hours), 16 to 18 years (6.5 hours) and 19 to 21 years (5.5 hours).

This bar chart shows the average daily screen time of students in four age groups. The highest figure is for students aged 16 to 18, who spend about six and a half hours a day on screens. In contrast, the youngest group, aged 10 to 12, spends only around three hours, which is less than half of that. Screen time rises sharply from 10 to 18 and then drops slightly to about five and a half hours for students aged 19 to 21. Overall, the chart suggests that screen use peaks in the late school years and falls a little once students reach college age.

Getting a high score in IELTS Reading is not about reading faster. It is about knowing how the questions are designed to mislead you, and having a method for each type. Many students from Kochi and across Kerala understand the passages well but still lose marks to the same traps: matching words instead of meaning, confusing False with Not Given, and running out of time on the last passage. These IELTS reading tips for 2026 cover the most common traps and exactly how to avoid them.
Know the test before you plan your strategy
The IELTS Academic Reading test has 40 questions on three sections, with a total text length of roughly 2,150 to 2,750 words. You have 60 minutes, and this includes the time to transfer your answers, so on paper there is no extra time at the end. On the computer-delivered test you type answers directly as you go. Each correct answer earns one mark, and your total is converted to a band score from 1 to 9.
General Training Reading also has 40 questions in 60 minutes, but the texts are taken from everyday and workplace sources such as notices, advertisements and handbooks. The traps described below apply to both versions.
IELTS reading tips for the most common traps
Trap 1: Matching keywords instead of meaning
IELTS almost always paraphrases. The words in the question are rarely the exact words in the passage, and when you do see an identical word, it is often a distractor placed near the wrong answer. Focus on the idea, not the word.



Question says
Passage might say

rose dramatically, soared, climbed steeply

not expensive
affordable, reasonably priced, low-cost


researchers believe
according to scientists, it is widely thought


at the beginning
initially, in its early stages, originally



Building this awareness takes practice. Our older post on the significance of keywords and synonyms in IELTS Reading has more examples.
Trap 2: Confusing False and Not Given
This is the trap that costs the most marks. The official definitions are clear:

True: the statement agrees with the information in the text.
False: the statement contradicts the information in the text.
Not Given: the statement neither agrees with nor contradicts the text.

Yes/No/Not Given questions work in the same way, but they test the writer’s views or claims rather than facts.
Worked example. Passage: “The bridge was completed in 1932, two years later than originally planned, and was at the time the longest of its kind in the region.”

The bridge was finished behind schedule. True (two years later than planned).
The bridge was completed in 1930. False (the text says 1932, a direct contradiction).
The bridge cost more than expected. Not Given (cost is never mentioned, even though delays often increase costs).

That last one is the classic trap: your own logic or general knowledge suggests an answer, but the passage does not say it. The official guidance specifically warns against using what you already know about the topic. If you cannot point to the words that prove or contradict the statement, it is Not Given.
Trap 3: Matching headings that echo a detail
In matching headings questions, there are always more headings than paragraphs, and wrong headings often describe a detail or example from the paragraph rather than its main idea.

Read the paragraph first, not the headings. Focus on the first two sentences and the last sentence.
Summarise the main idea in five or six words of your own.
Now find the heading that matches your summary.
Be suspicious of a heading that repeats a striking word from the middle of the paragraph.

Many Indian students have strong grammar knowledge from school, yet still lose marks in the TOEFL Writing section. The problem is usually not English itself but a set of predictable habits: formal phrases that sound odd in an email, essays with no clear opinion, and small slips that a careful reread would catch. This guide covers the most common TOEFL writing mistakes we see, with a fix for each, based on the current TOEFL iBT Writing tasks.
The TOEFL Writing section in 2026
Since January 2026, TOEFL iBT Writing takes about 23 minutes and has three task types:

Build a Sentence (10 items): arrange words or phrases into a correct sentence or question. Each item is worth 1 point.
Write an Email (1 item): write an email in an academic or social situation, such as making a request, giving information or proposing a solution. Scored out of 5.
Write for an Academic Discussion (1 item): add your opinion to an online class discussion and support it, responding to other students’ views. Scored out of 5.

The section result is reported on the new 1 to 6 band scale. ETS says scoring focuses on how clearly and effectively you communicate, not on producing a perfect first draft.
The most common TOEFL writing mistakes, and how to fix them
1. Preparing for the old format
Many free books and videos still teach the old integrated essay, where you read a passage and summarise a lecture. That task is no longer in the test. Fix: practise the three current tasks, using official ETS practice material wherever possible.
2. Overusing fancy vocabulary
Words like “plethora”, “myriad” or “paramount” used in the wrong context make writing harder to read, not more impressive. Fix: choose the clearest accurate word. Show range through precise everyday vocabulary (“affordable”, “reliable”, “time-consuming”) and varied sentence structures.
3. Ignoring part of the instructions
The email task usually lists several things to include. Students often answer two and forget the third. Fix: before typing, turn each instruction into a one-word checklist on your scratch paper and tick it off as you write.
4. The wrong tone in emails
Indian office English has phrases that read as strange or outdated to international readers:



Avoid
Use instead




Respected Sir/Madam
Dear Professor Thomas / Dear Ms Lee


Kindly do the needful
Could you please let me know …


Please revert back
I look forward to your reply


I am having a doubt
I have a question about …


Myself Arun, studying in …
My name is Arun, and I am a student in …



Fix: match the tone to the reader. A professor gets a polite, direct email; a classmate can get a friendlier one. Both should be clear and natural.
5. No clear position in the academic discussion
Some students describe both sides without ever saying what they think. Fix: state your opinion in your first or second sentence, such as “I agree with Priya that …” or “In my view, the better option is …”.
6. Repeating what classmates already said
The prompt shows posts from other students. Copying their reasons adds nothing. Fix: briefly acknowledge one classmate, then add a new reason or example of your own. This is what “responding to others’ viewpoints” means in practice.
7. General claims with no example
“Technology is very useful for students” says almost nothing. Fix: support each main point with a specific example, real or realistic: “When our college moved assignments to an online portal, I could submit work from home during the monsoon floods.”
8. Small grammar and spelling slips
The test is typed and has no spellchecker. Typical errors include:

Missing articles: “I am student” instead of “I am a student”.
Subject-verb agreement: “Each of the students have …” instead of “has”.
Extra prepositions: “discuss about”, “return back”, “comprise of”.
Uncountable nouns made plural: “informations”, “advices”, “equipments”.

A few years ago, almost every student in Kochi preparing to go abroad assumed IELTS was the only option. Today, many are choosing the PTE exam in Kerala instead, especially those heading to Australia or New Zealand. But PTE is not automatically the better test for everyone. This 2026 update looks at why PTE Academic has become so popular, where IELTS still makes more sense, and how to decide which one fits your plans.
What PTE Academic looks like in 2026
PTE Academic is a computer-based test from Pearson that checks speaking, writing, reading and listening in a single sitting of about two hours. It has three parts:

Speaking and Writing (about 76 to 84 minutes): tasks such as Read Aloud, Repeat Sentence, Describe Image, Retell Lecture, Answer Short Question, Summarize Written Text and Write Essay.
Reading (about 23 to 30 minutes).
Listening (about 31 to 39 minutes).

In 2025 Pearson added two new speaking tasks: Summarize Group Discussion, where you listen to three people discuss a topic and summarise it in your own words, and Respond to a Situation, where you give a spoken reply to an everyday scenario. If you are using older books or free videos, check that they include these tasks.
Scores are reported on a 10 to 90 scale, with a breakdown for each skill.
Why the PTE exam in Kerala is gaining ground
1. Fast results
Pearson says results typically arrive within two days. For students racing to meet a university deadline or a visa appointment, that speed is a real advantage. You can also share your scores with as many institutions as you need at no extra cost.
2. AI scoring with human checks
PTE uses AI scoring combined with human expertise. Many students like that the speaking section is not a face-to-face conversation, so the result does not depend on how one examiner feels on the day. The flip side is that the system rewards specific things, such as smooth fluency and covering the content, so you need to learn exactly what each task measures.
3. A speaking section that suits nervous speakers
You speak into a microphone, not to a person. Students who freeze in front of an examiner often find this less stressful. However, the speaking tasks are short and timed tightly, so hesitation costs marks quickly.
4. Wide acceptance, with some important details
PTE Academic is accepted by thousands of universities worldwide, including virtually all universities in Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the UK, and many in the US. Here is where the details matter:

Australia and New Zealand: PTE Academic is accepted for migration, work and study visas that need an English test.
Canada: universities accept PTE Academic for admission, but for permanent residency and citizenship applications IRCC uses PTE Core, a separate Pearson test.
UK: for work visas and study below degree level, you may need PTE Academic UKVI rather than the standard test.

Always confirm the exact test name your university, employer or visa category asks for before you book.
5. Frequent test dates
PTE offers regular test dates, often with last-minute slots. That flexibility helps working professionals and students who need a score quickly.
6. Typing instead of handwriting
All writing is typed. If you type quickly and accurately, the writing tasks can feel easier than handwriting a long essay. If you type slowly, practise early, because time pressure is real.
7. Strong coaching support in Kochi
As interest in the PTE exam in Kerala has grown, more trainers now understand how PTE scoring works task by task. Good coaching focuses on what the scoring actually rewards rather than generic English practice.

Whether you are taking IELTS Academic or General Training, grammar for IELTS writing is one of the four things the examiner scores. Grammatical Range and Accuracy is one of the four criteria for both Writing tasks, alongside Task Achievement or Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, and Lexical Resource. Many students we coach have good ideas and decent vocabulary, but small, repeated grammar errors hold their band back. Below are 10 rules that make the biggest difference, each with a short incorrect and correct example so you can check your own writing.
How grammar for IELTS writing is assessed
Examiners look at two things: range (whether you use a variety of sentence structures) and accuracy (how many errors you make and whether they affect meaning). A writer who only uses simple sentences will struggle to score highly on range, even if every sentence is correct. A writer who attempts very complex sentences full of errors will lose marks on accuracy. The aim is a natural mix of simple and complex sentences, written with control.
10 grammar rules for IELTS writing
1. Make subjects and verbs agree
Singular subjects take singular verbs, plural subjects take plural verbs. Watch out for long subjects where the main noun is far from the verb.

Incorrect: The number of students who study abroad have increased.
Correct: The number of students who study abroad has increased.
Incorrect: One of the main reason are cost.
Correct: One of the main reasons is cost.

2. Use the right tense, and keep it consistent
In Academic Task 1, match the tense to the time shown in the chart: past for past years, future forms for projections. In Task 2, use present tenses for general truths and present perfect for changes up to now.

Incorrect: In 2010, sales increase sharply and then they fell.
Correct: In 2010, sales increased sharply and then fell.
Incorrect: Technology changed our lives in recent years.
Correct: Technology has changed our lives in recent years.

3. Avoid sentence fragments
Every sentence needs a subject and a main verb. Fragments often start with “because”, “which” or “for example”.

Incorrect: Many people move to cities. Because there are more jobs.
Correct: Many people move to cities because there are more jobs.

4. Avoid run-on sentences and comma splices
The opposite problem: two complete sentences joined with only a comma. Use a full stop, a semicolon or a linking word.

Incorrect: Fast food is cheap, it is not healthy.
Correct: Fast food is cheap, but it is not healthy. or Fast food is cheap. However, it is not healthy.

5. Use articles (a, an, the) correctly
Article errors are among the most common for Indian learners because many Indian languages do not use articles in the same way. Use “a/an” for a singular countable noun mentioned for the first time, “the” for something specific or already mentioned, and no article for general plural or uncountable nouns.

Incorrect: Government should invest in the education.
Correct: The government should invest in education.
Incorrect: It is a important issue.
Correct: It is an important issue.

6. Get countable and uncountable nouns right
Words such as information, advice, research, equipment, furniture, knowledge and evidence are uncountable in English. They have no plural form and do not take “a/an”.

Incorrect: The internet gives many informations and advices.
Correct: The internet gives a lot of information and advice.
Incorrect: Several researches show this.
Correct: Several studies show this.

7. Keep lists and comparisons parallel
Items in a list, or two things being compared, should have the same grammatical form.

Correct: Students need reading, writing and listening skills.
Incorrect: Living in a city is more expensive than a village.
Correct: Living in a city is more expensive than living in a village.

Over the last two years, students from Kerala planning to study or work abroad have watched the rules change almost every few months. Canada capped study permits, the UK stopped most students from bringing family, Australia set limits on new enrolments and the US added extra checks for student visas. If you are preparing for IELTS, PTE or TOEFL right now, it is natural to ask whether your plans still make sense. This guide explains the main study visa changes for IELTS PTE TOEFL students, what they actually mean for your English test, and how to plan sensibly without panic.
One important point before we start: immigration rules are set by governments and they change often. Use this article to understand the direction of travel, then always confirm the current rules on the official immigration website of the country you are applying to before you pay any fees.
Why visas became harder to get
The slowdown is not about English tests becoming harder. It is about governments trying to reduce the number of temporary residents, ease pressure on housing and public services, and protect local job markets. A few common reasons appear across most popular destinations.

Record application numbers: Canada, Australia and the UK all saw very high numbers of international students around 2022 and 2023, which led to backlogs and tighter checks.
Housing and cost-of-living pressure: Governments linked fast growth in student numbers to rent and housing shortages, which made limits politically popular.
Concerns about low-quality courses: Several countries said some colleges were being used mainly as a route to work, not study, and tightened rules for those institutions.
Weaker job markets: Inflation and economic uncertainty reduced hiring in some sectors, so work visa routes became more selective.

Study visa changes for IELTS PTE TOEFL students: country by country
Here is a summary of the major changes that matter to test takers from India. Figures and dates are from official announcements at the time of writing; check the links to official sites at the end of this section before you apply.
Canada

Study permit cap: Canada introduced a national cap on study permits in 2024 and has continued it.
Provincial attestation letters (PAL): Most new college and undergraduate applicants need a letter from the province confirming they fit within its share of the cap. From January 2026, master’s and PhD students at public institutions no longer need one.
Post-graduation work permit (PGWP) language rule: Since November 2024, PGWP applicants must show English or French ability: CLB 7 for university degree graduates and CLB 5 for college graduates, in all four skills. Only IRCC-approved tests count for this, such as IELTS General Training, CELPIP or PTE Core. An IELTS Academic, PTE Academic or TOEFL score used for admission will not satisfy this rule.
Field of study rules: Graduates of many college programmes must now study in an eligible field to qualify for a PGWP.

If you are worried about costs as well, read our post on why tuition fees in Canada are rising and what alternatives IELTS aspirants have.
United Kingdom

Dependants: For courses starting on or after 1 January 2024, most international students can no longer bring a partner or children. Exceptions include research-based postgraduate degrees such as a PhD, and government-sponsored students.
Graduate visa: The UK Graduate visa currently lasts two years for those who apply on or before 31 December 2026. For applications on or after 1 January 2027, it drops to 18 months (PhD graduates still get three years).

Australia

Enrolment limits: Australia now sets a National Planning Level for new international students, with each provider given an allocation. The level for 2026 was announced as 295,000, slightly higher than 2025 but still well below the post-COVID peak.
Stricter checks: Visa officers look closely at whether you are a genuine student, your finances and your English test results.

Today, rising Canada tuition fees for Indian students, higher proof-of-funds rules and a cap on study permits mean the decision needs much more careful planning. Whether you are preparing for IELTS, PTE or TOEFL, this guide explains why studying in Canada costs more now, what the changes mean for your English test plans, and which alternatives are worth a look.
How much has tuition in Canada gone up?
Statistics Canada publishes average tuition fees every year. Its figures show that the average annual undergraduate tuition for international students in Canada has risen from about CAD 23,700 in 2016/2017 to about CAD 42,100 in 2026/2027. Over the same period, international students have come to pay several times what Canadian students pay for the same degree.

These are national averages. Fees vary a great deal by province, institution and course. Ontario has the highest average international undergraduate tuition, at around CAD 50,000 a year, while some Atlantic provinces are far lower. Professional programmes such as engineering, business and medicine usually cost more than arts or general science. Always check the exact fee on your institution’s website.
Tuition is only part of the bill. Accommodation, food, transport, health insurance and course materials add significantly to the yearly cost, particularly in large cities such as Toronto and Vancouver where rents are high.
Why are Canada tuition fees for Indian students rising?
Universities rely on international fees
Many Canadian colleges and universities have come to depend on international students to balance their budgets, as government funding has not kept pace with their costs. In many provinces, fees for international students are not regulated in the same way as fees for Canadian students, so institutions have more freedom to raise them.
Inflation and operating costs
Higher salaries, building maintenance, technology and general inflation have all increased the cost of running institutions, and part of that cost is passed on through tuition.
Fewer study permits
Since 2024 the Canadian government has capped the number of study permits it issues. With fewer international students, some institutions face financial pressure, which can affect both fees and the range of programmes on offer.
Other changes that raise the cost of studying in Canada

Higher proof of funds: study permit applicants must show they can cover living costs in addition to tuition and travel. IRCC raised this amount from CAD 10,000 to CAD 20,635 for a single applicant in January 2024, then to CAD 22,895 from September 2025, and it now reviews the figure every year. Check the current amount on the IRCC website before you apply.
End of the Student Direct Stream: the SDS, which many Indian students used for faster processing, closed on 8 November 2024. Applications now go through the regular study permit process.

e: You open the Writing paper, read the Task 2 question and your mind goes blank. The topic is space exploration, genetic engineering or the role of…

You open the Writing paper, read the Task 2 question and your mind goes blank. The topic is space exploration, genetic engineering or the role of museums, and you have never thought about it in your life. This happens to strong candidates too. The good news is that IELTS Writing Task 2 difficult topics are not testing your general knowledge. They test whether you can take an unfamiliar issue, form a clear position and support it in organised English. This guide shows you a repeatable method for handling those questions, with a worked example, and explains how the same approach works in Speaking Part 3.
Why some Task 2 topics feel so hard
In Task 2 you are given a point of view, argument or problem to discuss, and you must write at least 250 words. The official guidance suggests spending about 40 minutes on it, and Task 2 counts for twice as much as Task 1 in your Writing score. So a panic on a difficult topic can cost you a lot.
Topics usually feel difficult for one of three reasons:

Abstract ideas: questions about values, ethics, tradition or progress, with nothing concrete to hold on to.
Unfamiliar fields: science funding, urban planning, international aid or the arts.
Complex wording: two-part questions, or prompts that ask about one narrow aspect of a wide topic.

Remember what the examiner actually marks: Task Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. None of these criteria rewards expert knowledge. Simple, relevant ideas that are well developed will score better than clever ideas that are badly explained.
A five-step method for IELTS Writing Task 2 difficult topics
Step 1: Decode the question (2 minutes)
Underline the topic, the specific focus and the instruction. Ask: what exactly am I being asked to do? Is it agree or disagree, discuss both views, advantages and disadvantages, problem and solution, or a two-part question? The official IELTS guidance warns that if the question is about one aspect of a topic, you must write about that aspect only. Writing about “technology in general” when the question is about “technology in primary schools” is one of the fastest ways to lose Task Response marks.
Step 2: Generate ideas using familiar angles (3 minutes)
When you know nothing about a topic, run it through a quick checklist of angles that apply to almost anything:

People: individuals, families, children, the elderly
Money: cost, jobs, economy, taxes
Health and safety
Education and skills
Environment
Technology
Society and culture: tradition, identity, equality

You only need two strong ideas for a well-developed essay. Pick the two angles where you can explain a clear cause and effect.
Step 3: Decide your position and plan (3 to 5 minutes)
Choose a position you can defend easily, even if it is not your deepest personal belief. Then plan four paragraphs: introduction, two body paragraphs and a conclusion. Each body paragraph needs one main idea, an explanation and an example.
Step 4: Use specific, believable examples
Examples do not need to be statistics. A realistic example from your own experience or general knowledge is acceptable, and the official guidance says examples can come from your own experience. For instance, the way UPI payments spread across small shops in Kerala is a perfectly good example for an essay about technology and the economy. Avoid inventing precise figures, because made-up numbers often sound unconvincing.
Step 5: Write, then check (remaining time)
Write clearly and keep 3 to 4 minutes at the end to check for grammar slips, missing articles and repeated words. If you need help with this final check, see our list of grammar rules for IELTS writing.
Worked example: a difficult Task 2 question

Some people believe that governments should spend money on space exploration, while others think this money should be used to solve problems on Earth. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

Understanding the International English Language Testing System
IELTS, which stands for the International English Language Testing System, is one of the most popular English language proficiency tests in the world. It is recognized by over 10,000 organizations worldwide, including universities, employers, and governments. The exam assesses your abilities in four key areas and those are reading, writing, listening, and speaking.
If you are planning to study or work in an English speaking country like the UK, Australia, Canada, or New Zealand, IELTS is usually the preferred exam. Many universities and employers in these countries require applicants to take the IELTS exam as part of their application process.
Understanding the Pearson Test of English
On the other hand, the Pearson Test of English (PTE) is a relatively newer entrant in the English language proficiency exams. Developed by Pearson PLC, PTE is gaining popularity for its computer based format and fast results. Like IELTS, PTE also assesses your reading, writing, listening, and speaking skills.
For those who prefer a more modern and technology friendly exam experience, as one among the topPTE coaching centre Kochi, we can say that PTE is a great option. The exam is known for its unbiased scoring system and quick results, making it an attractive choice for many test takers.
The Relevance of Knowing the Difference
So, you may wonder what is the relevance of knowing the difference between PTE and IELTS. Understanding the unique aspects of each exam can help you make a decision on which test to take based on your preferences and end goal.
The Key Factors to Consider
Format: IELTS is a paper based exam, while PTE is a computer based test. If you are more comfortable typing on a computer than writing by hand, PTE might be the better option for you.
Scoring: Both IELTS and PTE use a scoring system to assess your proficiency level in English. However, the scoring criteria and scale may vary between the two exams. It is essential to familiarize yourself with the scoring system of each exam to understand how your performance will be evaluated.
Test Dates and Availability: IELTS is offered in over 1,200 locations worldwide, while PTE is available in over 200 locations globally. Depending on your location and schedule, you may find it easier to access one exam over the other.

Both IELTS and PTE are valuable exams that can open doors to study or work opportunities abroad. Expected Errors during IELTS Listening Exams

Don’t ignore the given instructions –If you are reading the instructions as answer in not more than two words, you must answer it accordingly. Otherwise, you will not score for that question.
Don’t leave blank – Even if you don’t know the answer you must give a guess answer. You won’t be getting negative marks for wrong responses.
Avoid spelling or grammatical mistakes – Any answer that is given with wrong spelling or if it is grammatically incorrect, it will be marked wrong. So you must listen to the audio before giving the response.
Don’t write on the answer sheet while you listen.

Expected Errors during IELTS Reading Exams

Maintain word formatting – In the IELTS exams, it is recommended to write either in all capital letters or in all small letters.
Don’t read the passage completely – Here you must use the skim and scan method. You must try finding the relevant keywords and connectors, and then skim the text for getting idea about the topic. This will help you to avoid unnecessary words and information from the passage.
Don’t lose focus on the order of questions – Generally, the questions will be in the same order as the text. Thus, if you get 2nd and 4th answer then you must find your 3rd answer somewhere between those two answers.
Don’t fail into the trap of complex vocabularies – If you can’t find the meaning then it is better to move.

Expected Errors in IELTS Writing Exams

Don’t write unnecessary words – Sometimes aspirants will write more words than given in the instructions. This can affect your marks.
Know when to write in first person
Time Management
Don’t change the topic – You have to strictly write on the topic that is given in the exam.

Expected Errors in IELTS Speaking Exam

Don’t repeat the question asked by the examiner.
Try not to speak with a flat intonation – For maintaining the listener’s interest you must vary your pitch, volume, speed, and intonation.
Don’t use advanced vocabulary – Don’t complicate it for yourself, if you are comfortable using advanced vocabulary you can go with it.
Speak according to requirements.

Test Structure
There are two modules of the IELTS – Academic module and General Training Module. Similarly, there is also a separate test offered by the IELTS test partners, which is called IELTS Life Skills.

The IELTS Academic is for those who want to enroll in universities and other institutions of higher education. This is also intended for professionals such as medical doctors and nurses who are willing to study or practice in any English- speaking countries.
IELTS General Training is meant for those planning to undertake some kind of non-academic training. It is also useful to gain work experience or for any immigration purposes.
IELTS Life Skills are for those who need to prove their English Speaking skills at the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR).

Four Parts of IELTS Tests
The IELTS test has four parts with a test total time of 2 hours and 45 minutes. The Casper Academy is best IELTS coaching centre in Kochi to give intensive training. The four parts include:

Listening test: 30 minutes (with 10 minutes transfer time)
Reading test: 60 minutes
Writing test: 60 minutes
Speaking: 11-14 minutes

Here the listening, reading, and writing tests are taken at once. Also the test takers will take the same listening and speaking tests. Similarly reading and writing tests differ depending on whether they are taking Academic or General Training.

Listening – The module comprises four sections with having ten questions in both section. It will have sections like a conversation between two speakers, one person speaking, a conversation between two main speakers, and one person speaking about an academic subject.
Reading –The reading paper is of three sections. The reading texts are coming  from books, journals, magazines, newspapers, and online resources that are written for non-specialist audiences.
Writing – The writing paper has two tasks. Here the test takers must describe a graph, table, map, process, pie chart or diagram in their own words. In the other task they must describe a point of view, argument or a problem.
Speaking – The speaking test is the face-to-face interview between the test taker and examiner. It contains sections like introduction and interview, giving task card about a particular topic and discussion relating to the theme.
